cards.front: What is the identity linking TVPI, DPI, and RVPI?
cards.back: TVPI = DPI + RVPI. Total value per dollar in equals realized cash plus unrealized NAV per dollar in.

cards.front: Which return metric cannot be marked up by the GP, and why does it dominate LP focus in 2025–2026?
cards.back: DPI, because it counts only cash actually distributed. Exits stalled, so GPs sit on large unrealized marks, making realized cash the credible signal. 2018-vintage DPI is running around 0.6x versus a historical norm near 0.8x.

cards.front: A fund shows 25% IRR but only 1.4x MOIC. What does that pattern suggest?
cards.back: Fast, modest-magnitude returns or timing effects (early partial exits, dividend recaps, subscription-line use). High IRR with low multiple is the fingerprint of financial engineering rather than durable value creation.

cards.front: Why does a subscription line raise IRR but not MOIC?
cards.back: It delays the LP capital call, shortening the period the LP's cash is at work, which raises the time-weighted IRR. Total dollars returned are unchanged except for the interest cost, which slightly lowers the multiple.

cards.front: Define the capital loss ratio and give a rough buyout benchmark.
cards.back: Percent of invested capital in deals realized below cost, net of recoveries, over total invested capital. US buyout clusters around the low-double-digit (roughly 10%) range; VC is far higher.

cards.front: Name the three levers of the value-creation bridge and which signals real skill.
cards.back: EBITDA growth (operating skill), multiple expansion (mostly beta/timing), and deleveraging (leverage). EBITDA growth is the skill signal.

cards.front: What did McKinsey find about the sources of buyout return for deals entered 2010+ and exited by 2021?
cards.back: Roughly two-thirds of total return came from multiple expansion and leverage, not operating improvement. Bain's 2026 framing: 'twelve is the new five,' meaning deals now require far faster EBITDA growth.

cards.front: Differentiate a European from an American distribution waterfall.
cards.back: European (whole-fund): carry only after all capital plus pref is returned across the fund — LP-friendly, the default. American (deal-by-deal): carry as each deal exits — GP-friendly, requires a strong clawback.

cards.front: What three features determine whether a clawback is actually protective?
cards.back: Whether it is escrow-backed, computed gross rather than net of the GP's taxes, and joint-and-several across partners rather than merely several.

cards.front: What is the difference between a hard and a soft hurdle?
cards.back: Hard hurdle: carry applies only to returns above the hurdle. Soft hurdle: once cleared, the catch-up lets the GP earn carry on all profits including the hurdle portion.

cards.front: Compute the GP catch-up for a 100% catch-up, 20% carry, where LPs have received $20M of preferred return.
cards.back: X = (0.20 × 20) / (1 − 0.20) = 4 / 0.8 = $5M. The GP receives $5M so that it holds exactly 20% of all profit distributed so far.

cards.front: Why does ILPA prefer the GP commitment funded in cash rather than via fee waiver?
cards.back: Cash is real personal capital at risk (alignment); a fee waiver is merely foregone fee, which is not skin in the game.

cards.front: What does a key-person trigger typically do, and what lifts it?
cards.back: It suspends the investment period (no new deployment) when named principals leave or stop devoting time; LP or LPAC supermajority consent (often within a 90–180-day cure window) lifts it.

cards.front: Why is a no-fault divorce clause a deterrent even though it is almost never used?
cards.back: Because removal requires no proof of wrongdoing and no litigation, a GP that knows a supermajority of LPs can terminate it behaves more cooperatively on fees, conflicts, and disclosure.

cards.front: What no-fault removal threshold do sources cite, and where do they disagree?
cards.back: Commonly 66.7% to 85% in interest; ILPA standard often cited as 75%. GP-drafted LPAs push to 80%+, which is effectively toothless in a diversified LP base.

cards.front: State the three ILPA Principles 3.0 pillars.
cards.back: Alignment of interest, governance, and transparency.

cards.front: What is the ILPA-recommended fee offset percentage and why?
cards.back: 100%, so transaction/monitoring/director fees the GP collects reduce the management fee dollar-for-dollar. Less than 100% means LPs effectively pay twice.

cards.front: Distinguish IDD from ODD in one line each.
cards.back: IDD: can you generate returns (strategy, team, track record). ODD: can we trust you with our capital (administration, valuation, compliance, cyber, controls).

cards.front: Why can the ODD team veto a commitment the investment team loves?
cards.back: Roughly half of manager failures are operational (fraud, valuation, controls) rather than investment-driven. A clean investment case does not survive a failed ODD.

cards.front: Name two structural ODD red flags that enabled historical frauds.
cards.back: No independent third-party administrator (GP self-administers and self-values) and no segregation of duties (one person controls deals, valuation, and cash). Madoff and Bayou are canonical cautionary tales.

cards.front: What is a KS-PME of 1.18 telling you?
cards.back: LPs ended with about 18% more wealth than the same cash flows invested in the chosen public index at the same times; the fund beat the index net of fees.

cards.front: Why does index choice matter as much as PME method?
cards.back: Because alpha is measured against the chosen benchmark. A large-cap fund should be measured against the S&P 500, a small-cap fund against the Russell 2000, a tech/growth fund against the Nasdaq — or the alpha is mis-stated.

cards.front: Summarize the Kaplan-Schoar 2005 vs. Harris-Jenkinson-Kaplan 2014 disagreement on PE performance.
cards.back: KS (2005, Venture Economics data) found average buyout roughly matched the S&P 500 net of fees (PME ~0.97). HJK (2014, Burgiss data) found buyout outperformed by ~20%–27% over a fund's life. Cleaner data raised the estimate.

cards.front: What is the modern evidence on buyout performance persistence?
cards.back: It has weakened since 2000: prior-fund quartile is a poor predictor of the next fund's quartile for buyout. What persists more reliably is the bottom (poor performers stay poor or fail to raise). VC persistence is stronger.

cards.front: How should 'top-quartile' claims be verified?
cards.back: Pin the GP to a named benchmark, the exact vintage, and the exact strategy. Do not allow a fund to be compared against a different-vintage benchmark.

cards.front: What is strategy/size drift and why does it gut the value of a track record?
cards.back: Departing from the strategy that built the record (bigger funds, new sectors/geographies, higher leverage). The historical returns were generated by the old strategy, so they barely predict the new one — you are effectively backing a first-time fund with a misleading halo.

cards.front: What does it mean if a fund's 2.4x TVPI falls to 1.3x after removing its single best deal?
cards.back: The record is concentrated in one outcome rather than a repeatable process. You are underwriting luck, and must judge whether the GP can repeat it.

cards.front: What does it signal if a GP's marks did not move through the 2022–2023 public drawdown?
cards.back: NAV smoothing: sticky marks that understate volatility and prop up TVPI/RVPI. Haircut the unrealized value and re-underwrite.

cards.front: Roughly what gross-to-net spread is typical for a successful buyout fund?
cards.back: About 5–7 points of IRR and 0.4x–0.6x of MOIC. Net TVPI captures roughly 75%–85% of gross MOIC.

cards.front: What is the J-curve and why does early DPI look bad?
cards.back: Early in a fund's life, fees and costs hit before investments appreciate or exit, so NAV and DPI dip first and rise later. Near-zero year-3 DPI is normal.

cards.front: What DPI would worry you for a year-7 buyout fund, and what is a healthy mature target?
cards.back: Below roughly 0.5x at year 7 raises questions. Mature (year 10–12) top-quartile funds end above ~2.0x, with ~1.5x+ expected by year 8. Always benchmark to the same vintage cohort.

cards.front: What is the ILPA recommendation on subscription-line preferred-return accrual?
cards.back: The preferred return should accrue from the date the credit facility is drawn, not the later date capital is called from LPs, so the line cannot be used to hand the GP an easier hurdle.

cards.front: Why is the GP commitment's distribution across partners as important as its size?
cards.back: If one partner funds most of the commitment and holds most of the carry, the rest of the team is weakly retained and key-person risk is concentrated regardless of the headline percentage.

cards.front: Why are continuation vehicles / GP-led secondaries conflict-laden, and what protections do LPs demand?
cards.back: The same GP sits on both sides (selling from the old fund, buying into the new vehicle), so price can favor the GP. LPs demand LPAC approval, an independent fairness opinion, and a genuine option to cash out or roll.

cards.front: In the current market, why discount a GP whose returns came mostly from multiple expansion and leverage?
cards.back: Cheap debt and easy multiple expansion are gone. Bain frames it as 'twelve is the new five,' meaning deals now require far faster EBITDA growth, so a beta-and-leverage track record is unlikely to repeat.
